bullets.label: Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing II — "Manage complexity with confidence."

cards.title: About This Programme
cards.body: GNPS Program 5 builds on the assessment and care-planning skills developed in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing I. The focus now moves to adults with acute, unstable or complex conditions that can deteriorate rapidly and require timely, coordinated nursing action.

bullets.label: This level introduces advanced assessment,
bullets.text: This level introduces advanced assessment, emergency priorities, multiorgan risk and evidence-based nursing interventions — while reinforcing the importance of practising within scope and escalating early.

bullets.label: Identify high-acuity adult medical-surgical presentations early.
Use safety-first and ABC frameworks in urgent clinical situations.
Read vital-sign trends and clinical findings accurately.
Act on deterioration and communicate clearly within the multidisciplinary team.

cards.title: Why This Learning Matters
cards.body: Complex illness affects multiple body systems simultaneously. A patient with sepsis may develop respiratory distress, hypotension, kidney injury and altered consciousness within a single shift.

bullets.label: Nurses must recognise patterns, identify the
bullets.text: Nurses must recognise patterns, identify the immediate threat, and act before deterioration becomes irreversible. This programme gives you that capability.

bullets.label: Your Learning Goal: By the end of Level 1, you
bullets.text: Your Learning Goal: By the end of Level 1, you should be able to recognise, prioritise, and respond safely to common high-acuity adult conditions and contribute effectively to multidisciplinary emergency management.

bullets.label: Identifying the most urgent threat — before addressing the full clinical picture.
Identify threats to ABC immediately. Call for
bullets.text: Identify threats to ABC immediately. Call for assistance and begin scope-appropriate actions while activating the emergency response.

bullets.label: Rising RR, falling BP, reduced urine output,
bullets.text: Rising RR, falling BP, reduced urine output, elevated lactate or altered consciousness together signal decompensation — one number alone is rarely enough.

bullets.label: Unexpected changes — sudden neuro shift
bullets.text: Unexpected changes — sudden neuro shift post-surgery or new chest pain — require immediate reassessment and escalation, not a wait-and-see approach.

bullets.label: After every intervention — oxygen, fluids,
bullets.text: After every intervention — oxygen, fluids, positioning, medication — reassess. Improvement, no change, or worsening each dictates the next action.

bullets.label: During the shift, Mr Kumar becomes restless, tachycardic and hypotensive with falling urine output.
The nurse recognises a pattern of circulatory
bullets.text: The nurse recognises a pattern of circulatory compromise rather than treating each finding separately — initiates the deterioration pathway and prepares for urgent review.

bullets.label: Prioritise immediate threats before routine care
Interpret combinations and trends, not isolated numbers
Treat unexpected changes as clinically significant
Early recognition, oxygenation, circulation, monitoring and timely escalation.
Chest pressure, diaphoresis, nausea,
bullets.text: Chest pressure, diaphoresis, nausea, breathlessness or ECG change. Immediate monitoring, prescribed emergency treatment and rapid escalation are essential.

bullets.label: Irregular rhythms reduce cardiac output. Acute
bullets.text: Irregular rhythms reduce cardiac output. Acute heart failure causes breathlessness, crackles and fluid overload. Monitor rhythm, perfusion and oxygenation.

bullets.label: Silent chest, inability to speak, exhaustion or
bullets.text: Silent chest, inability to speak, exhaustion or altered consciousness demand immediate escalation and emergency airway support — do not wait for further deterioration.

bullets.label: Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, hypoxia or
bullets.text: Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, hypoxia or tachycardia may indicate PE. ARDS produces severe oxygenation failure requiring urgent multidisciplinary management.

bullets.label: A patient being treated for asthma becomes
bullets.text: A patient being treated for asthma becomes quieter, with reduced air entry and increasing drowsiness. Although wheezing has decreased, the nurse recognises this may indicate exhaustion rather than improvement and activates urgent medical review.

bullets.label: Reduced symptoms do not always mean improvement
bullets.text: Reduced symptoms do not always mean improvement — fatigue and altered consciousness are late and dangerous respiratory signs.

bullets.label: Escalate sudden breathlessness or chest pain urgently
Rapid changes in consciousness, circulation and electrolyte balance demand immediate action.
Facial weakness, speech difficulty, limb
bullets.text: Facial weakness, speech difficulty, limb weakness or visual change may indicate stroke. During a seizure, protect the airway, time the event and observe recovery.

bullets.label: Declining consciousness, vomiting, unequal
bullets.text: Declining consciousness, vomiting, unequal pupils or severe headache may indicate raised intracranial pressure. Avoid any delay in escalation.

bullets.label: AKI may present with reduced urine output,
bullets.text: AKI may present with reduced urine output, fluid overload or acidosis. Severe potassium, sodium or calcium changes can affect cardiac and neurological function.

bullets.label: DKA, HHS, thyroid storm and myxoedema coma can
bullets.text: DKA, HHS, thyroid storm and myxoedema coma can all be life-threatening. Monitor glucose, fluids, electrolytes, temperature, consciousness and treatment response.

bullets.label: A patient with diabetes develops deep rapid breathing (Kussmaul), abdominal pain, dehydration and increasing drowsiness.
The nurse suspects DKA — checks glucose and
bullets.text: The nurse suspects DKA — checks glucose and ketones, begins the emergency pathway and monitors fluid, electrolyte and neurological status continuously.

bullets.label: Treat sudden neurological change as an emergency
Monitor urine output as a key perfusion indicator
Follow emergency protocols while reassessing continuously
Early recognition and rapid treatment save lives — nurses are often first to notice.
Sepsis can progress to multiorgan failure within hours. Recognise, escalate, intervene and monitor without delay.
Ms Lee has a urinary infection and becomes
bullets.text: Ms Lee has a urinary infection and becomes confused, tachypnoeic and hypotensive. The nurse recognises sepsis with possible shock, activates the emergency pathway, obtains observations and specimens, and monitors response closely.

bullets.label: Act on suspected sepsis before severe collapse occurs
Use perfusion and organ-function indicators together
Communicate trends and treatment response clearly

cards.title: Programme Complete — What's Next?
cards.body: By completing GNPS Program 5 · Level 1, you have developed essential skills in advanced assessment, urgent prioritisation and nursing care for high-acuity adult conditions.

bullets.label: Advanced assessment, ABC frameworks,
bullets.text: Advanced assessment, ABC frameworks, cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological, renal, endocrine, sepsis and shock management.

bullets.label: Complex interpretation, high-risk therapies and
bullets.text: Complex interpretation, high-risk therapies and international acute-care practice for the internationally qualified nurse.

bullets.label: These capabilities directly support NCLEX
bullets.text: These capabilities directly support NCLEX preparation — particularly the Management of Care, Physiological Adaptation and Reduction of Risk Potential client needs categories.

decks.title: Advanced Assessment & Clinical Prioritisation
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 5 - Level 1 - Section 1 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

bullets.label: Patients with complex conditions often present
bullets.text: Patients with complex conditions often present with multiple abnormal findings simultaneously. This section equips you with the tools to assess rapidly, prioritise effectively, and reassess continuously.

cards.title: Why Advanced Assessment Matters
cards.body: In complex clinical situations, the ability to identify the most immediate threat — while maintaining awareness of the full clinical picture — is the hallmark of advanced nursing practice. Rapid assessment must always be followed by focused reassessment after every intervention.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Systematically evaluate Airway, Breathing, and Circulation in any acutely unwell patient.
Differentiate findings that require immediate escalation from those that can be monitored.
Identify clinical trends that signal a patient is decompensating before a crisis occurs.
Decide what to do first, second, and when to call for urgent assistance in complex situations.

cards.title: Core Concept: Airway, Breathing and Circulation
cards.body: ABC forms the foundation of every rapid nursing assessment. When any of these systems is compromised:

bullets.label: Identify the threat quickly and systematically
Begin actions within your scope of practice
Never delay escalation while gathering more information. Act first, document fully afterwards.

cards.title: Reading Clinical Trends
cards.body: A single abnormal result may be less significant than a worsening pattern. Always interpret findings in context and over time.

bullets.label: Early warning of hypoxia or metabolic distress
May indicate haemorrhage, sepsis, or cardiac compromise
Signals renal hypoperfusion and fluid deficit
Critical indicator of cerebral or systemic decompensation
Consistent with the known condition or the
bullets.text: Consistent with the known condition or the expected stage of recovery. These can be monitored within the standard care plan.

bullets.label: Mild post-operative pain, controlled by analgesia
Slight elevation in temperature on day one post-op
Gradual improvement in oxygen saturation with supplemental O₂
Require immediate reassessment and escalation. Do not wait for the routine observation round.
New chest pain in a patient recovering from infection
Unexplained drop in SpO₂ despite no change in therapy
Reassessment is not optional — it is a core
bullets.text: Reassessment is not optional — it is a core nursing responsibility. After every intervention, the nurse must evaluate the patient's response and determine the next appropriate action.

bullets.label: Continue current plan. Document response. Set next reassessment time.
Review the intervention. Consider additional measures. Consult if uncertain.
Escalate immediately. Activate deterioration pathway. Prepare for urgent review.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Mr Kumar
cards.body: A patient admitted with pancreatitis becomes restless, tachycardic, and hypotensive during the shift. His urine output begins to fall.

bullets.label: Rather than treating each abnormal finding in
bullets.text: Rather than treating each abnormal finding in isolation, the nurse recognises a pattern of circulatory compromise. She initiates the deterioration pathway, calls for urgent review, and prepares for possible fluid resuscitation — all within her scope of practice.

bullets.label: Tachycardia — compensatory response to falling output
Recognised the pattern, not just individual numbers

cards.title: Pattern Recognition: The Advanced Nurse's Edge
cards.body: Advanced nursing is not about memorising individual thresholds — it is about recognising clinical pictures. Skilled nurses integrate multiple data points to detect decompensation before it becomes a crisis.

bullets.label: Consider the patient's baseline and trajectory
Cluster findings rather than treating them in isolation
Use early warning scores as a structured tool
Trust clinical intuition — then verify with objective data

cards.title: NCLEX Focus: Priority Questions
cards.body: NCLEX frequently tests your ability to prioritise. Apply the ABCs and Maslow's hierarchy to determine the correct sequence of action.

bullets.label: Always address airway obstruction before any other concern, regardless of how urgent other findings appear.
Stabilise the physical threat before addressing psychological or comfort needs.
When managing multiple patients, attend to the most haemodynamically unstable patient first.
An existing problem takes priority over a risk — unless the risk represents an immediate life threat.
Address life-threatening problems before moving to routine care tasks.
Isolated numbers are less meaningful than a cluster of worsening findings over time.
Never dismiss a sudden or unexplained change — it demands immediate reassessment.
Evaluation is continuous — the clinical picture changes with every action taken.
You are now equipped to approach complex patients with a structured, confident mindset. Remember:
Use the ABC framework to identify immediate threats.
Act on the most critical finding first.
Every intervention demands a follow-up evaluation.

decks.title: Cardiovascular & Respiratory Emergencies
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 5 - Level 1 - Section 2 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

bullets.label: Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing II — Section 2: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Emergencies

cards.title: Manage Complexity with Confidence
cards.body: Acute cardiovascular and respiratory emergencies can deteriorate rapidly. This section equips nurses with the knowledge to act decisively — from early recognition to timely escalation.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Identify common cardiac and respiratory emergency presentations promptly.
Detect signs of haemodynamic instability and respiratory deterioration.
Apply immediate, evidence-based interventions with confidence.
Track response to treatment and anticipate potential complications.

cards.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)
cards.body: ACS encompasses a spectrum of life-threatening myocardial ischaemia conditions — including unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI.

bullets.label: Chest pressure or tightness — often radiating to jaw or left arm
Breathlessness at rest or with minimal exertion
ECG changes — ST elevation, depression, T-wave inversion
Atypical presentations are common in women, older adults, and diabetic patients. Stay vigilant.
Rapid, structured nursing response within the
bullets.text: Rapid, structured nursing response within the first minutes of ACS presentation significantly improves patient outcomes and reduces myocardial damage.

cards.title: Arrhythmias and Acute Heart Failure
cards.body: Abnormal cardiac rhythms and decompensated heart failure both impair cardiac output — threatening organ perfusion and requiring swift nursing recognition.

bullets.label: AF, SVT, VT — rapid rhythms reducing diastolic filling and cardiac output
Complete heart block, sinus bradycardia — slow rhythms causing hypoperfusion
Orthopnoea, bilateral crackles, hypoxia, oedema — fluid overload in failure
Assess perfusion: skin, urine output, consciousness
Oxygen saturation and work of breathing
Response to prescribed diuretics or rate-control agents

cards.title: Pulmonary Embolism and ARDS
cards.body: Both conditions represent severe threats to oxygenation — one from vascular obstruction, the other from diffuse lung injury. Early recognition is life-saving.

bullets.label: Continuous monitoring of respiratory rate and effort
Position patient upright to optimise lung expansion
IV access and urgent bloods including D-dimer, ABG
Escalate immediately to senior clinician and MDT
Unable to speak in full sentences
Silent chest — absent wheeze despite distress
Exhaustion — use of accessory muscles, fatigue
Deteriorating blood gases — rising CO₂, falling pH
A silent chest is a medical emergency. Absent wheeze ≠ improvement.
Identify red flag signs: silent chest, exhaustion, altered GCS
Administer oxygen, assist positioning, support work of breathing
Activate emergency review — call senior nurse, doctor, or rapid response team
Continuous SpO₂, RR, consciousness, response to treatment

cards.title: Clinical Scenario: The Quietening Asthma Patient
cards.body: A patient being treated for acute asthma becomes quieter. Air entry is reduced. The patient appears increasingly drowsy. Wheezing has decreased — but the nurse correctly identifies this as exhaustion, not improvement.

bullets.label: The nurse activates an urgent medical review immediately
Silent chest + fatigue = impending respiratory arrest risk
Reduced symptoms do not always mean improvement — assess the whole picture.
Monitor peripheral perfusion alongside cardiac rhythm — both reflect cardiac output.
Sudden breathlessness or chest pain demands urgent escalation. Do not delay.
Fatigue and altered consciousness are late — and dangerous — respiratory warning signs.

cards.title: Section 2 Complete
cards.body: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Emergencies — GNPS Programme 5

bullets.label: You are now equipped to recognise, respond to,
bullets.text: You are now equipped to recognise, respond to, and escalate life-threatening cardiac and respiratory emergencies with evidence-based nursing practice.

cards.title: Neurological, Renal & Endocrine Emergencies
cards.body: GNPS Programme 5 · Advanced Adult Nursing Care — Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing II

cards.title: Programme Overview
cards.body: This section is part of the Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) — designed to help internationally qualified nurses build clinical confidence and prepare for the NCLEX examination.

bullets.label: GNPS Programme 5 — Advanced Adult Nursing Care

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Recognise signs of stroke, seizure and raised intracranial pressure
Identify acute kidney injury and dangerous electrolyte disturbances
Recognise diabetic emergencies and thyroid crises
Implement immediate safety measures and continuous monitoring

cards.title: Stroke & Seizures
cards.body: Recognising the difference between stroke and seizure is a critical nursing skill. Both demand immediate action.

bullets.label: Use the FAST tool — Face, Arms, Speech, Time — and escalate immediately.
Protect the airway and prevent injury
Position patient safely — do not restrain
Observe and document the recovery phase
Raised ICP is a life-threatening emergency. Do not delay escalation.
Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations
Any deterioration in consciousness demands urgent escalation — every minute matters.
Reduced urine output (<0.5 ml/kg/hr), fluid
bullets.text: Reduced urine output (<0.5 ml/kg/hr), fluid overload, rising creatinine, and metabolic acidosis are hallmark signs of acute kidney injury.

bullets.label: Hyperkalaemia can cause life-threatening
bullets.text: Hyperkalaemia can cause life-threatening arrhythmias. Monitor ECG changes: peaked T waves, widened QRS, and flat P waves.

bullets.label: Severe hypo- or hypernatraemia impairs
bullets.text: Severe hypo- or hypernatraemia impairs neurological function. Hypocalcaemia causes tetany and seizures. Frequent lab monitoring is essential.

bullets.label: Diabetic Ketoacidosis — hyperglycaemia, ketones, deep rapid (Kussmaul) breathing, dehydration, acidosis
Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State — extreme
bullets.text: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State — extreme hyperglycaemia, severe dehydration, altered consciousness, no significant ketosis

bullets.label: High fever, tachycardia, hypertension,
bullets.text: High fever, tachycardia, hypertension, agitation — life-threatening hyperthyroid crisis requiring urgent medical intervention

bullets.label: Severe hypothyroidism — hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, reduced consciousness — treat as a medical emergency
In all endocrine emergencies, nurses must
bullets.text: In all endocrine emergencies, nurses must closely monitor glucose, fluids, electrolytes, temperature, consciousness and treatment response.

bullets.label: A patient with known diabetes presents with
bullets.text: A patient with known diabetes presents with deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul respirations), abdominal pain, signs of dehydration, and increasing drowsiness.

bullets.label: The nurse suspects Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) and acts immediately.
Measure bedside glucose and ketone levels.
Notify medical team and escalate care immediately.
Track fluids, electrolytes, and neuro status.

cards.title: NCLEX Focus: Key Principles to Remember

bullets.label: Any sudden deterioration in consciousness,
bullets.text: Any sudden deterioration in consciousness, speech or motor function must be treated as an emergency until proven otherwise.

bullets.label: Urine Output is a Perfusion Indicator
Monitor urine output as a key sign of renal and
bullets.text: Monitor urine output as a key sign of renal and circulatory function. Less than 0.5 ml/kg/hr demands immediate assessment.

bullets.label: Always link electrolyte imbalances to cardiac
bullets.text: Always link electrolyte imbalances to cardiac risk. Potassium disturbances in particular are directly associated with life-threatening rhythms.

bullets.label: Follow emergency protocols, but reassess continuously. Patient status can change rapidly — never assume stability.
You have covered the essential clinical
bullets.text: You have covered the essential clinical knowledge for neurological, renal and endocrine emergencies. Apply these principles in practice and revisit them as you prepare for the NCLEX examination.

bullets.label: Proceed to Section 4 of GNPS Programme 5
Revisit the clinical example and key learning points
Practise NCLEX-style questions on this section's topics

decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 5 - Level 1 - Section 4 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Sepsis, Shock & Multisystem Deterioration
cards.body: Section 4 · Level 1 – Qualified Nurse | Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) Programme 5: Advanced Adult Nursing Care

bullets.label: Sepsis and shock can progress rapidly to
bullets.text: Sepsis and shock can progress rapidly to multiorgan failure. Early recognition and decisive action are the cornerstones of survival.

bullets.label: Nurses are often the first to recognise the
bullets.text: Nurses are often the first to recognise the critical combination of infection, altered perfusion, and organ dysfunction — making clinical vigilance a life-saving skill.

bullets.label: This section equips you with the knowledge to act swiftly and systematically when it matters most.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Identify the clinical indicators that signal rapid deterioration before collapse occurs.
Distinguish between hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive and obstructive shock.
Follow emergency pathways accurately and assist with urgent treatment without delay.
Track systemic deterioration and communicate trends clearly to the clinical team.
Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction
bullets.text: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. It demands urgent clinical assessment and must never be delayed.

bullets.label: Suspect sepsis when a possible infection is present alongside any two or more of the following new-onset signs:
Altered mental status or sudden disorientation
Shock is a state of inadequate tissue perfusion
bullets.text: Shock is a state of inadequate tissue perfusion leading to cellular dysfunction. Identifying the type of shock guides appropriate treatment.

bullets.label: Caused by blood or fluid loss (haemorrhage, severe dehydration). Most common type in trauma and surgical settings.
Heart fails to pump adequately, often following myocardial infarction or severe arrhythmia.
Abnormal vasodilation with maldistribution of blood flow — septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic shock fall here.
Physical obstruction to circulation — pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade or tension pneumothorax.

cards.title: Common Signs of Shock
cards.body: Regardless of type, shock shares a recognisable cluster of clinical signs that nurses must identify promptly:

bullets.label: Confusion, agitation, reduced responsiveness — early signs of cerebral hypoperfusion.
Mottling, pallor, prolonged capillary refill (>2 seconds), cold and clammy skin.
Heart rate >100 bpm — compensatory response to reduced cardiac output.
Systolic BP <90 mmHg — a late and serious sign indicating decompensation.
Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) signals inadequate renal perfusion and impending organ failure.

cards.title: Time-Critical Care
cards.body: Every minute matters. Following emergency pathways swiftly and accurately is essential in sepsis and shock management.

cards.title: Emergency Response
cards.body: The Sepsis Bundle: Acting Without Delay

bullets.label: Time to antimicrobial therapy is one of the
bullets.text: Time to antimicrobial therapy is one of the strongest predictors of patient survival in septic shock. Each step must be completed without delay.

bullets.label: Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics where possible
Administer prescribed antimicrobials within the target window
Apply supplemental oxygen and monitor SpO₂
Insert IV access — large-bore cannula preferred
Administer IV fluid bolus as directed (typically 500 mL crystalloid)
Measure serum lactate and repeat to monitor response
Document all actions with accurate timestamps
Always follow your local clinical protocol. Pathway adherence saves lives.
When sepsis or shock is not controlled, organ
bullets.text: When sepsis or shock is not controlled, organ systems begin to fail — often in a predictable pattern. Nurses must monitor and escalate deteriorating trends early.

bullets.label: Rising O₂ requirements, falling SpO₂, increased respiratory rate — risk of ARDS
Falling urine output, rising creatinine — acute kidney injury risk
Persistent hypotension, tachycardia, vasopressor requirement escalation
Rising bilirubin, coagulopathy — signs of liver dysfunction
Worsening confusion, reduced GCS — indicates inadequate cerebral perfusion
Accurate documentation and structured
bullets.text: Accurate documentation and structured communication are critical. Use SBAR or your local escalation framework to convey trends — not just single observations — to the team.

bullets.label: Who is the patient and what is happening right now?
Relevant history, diagnosis, treatment to date
Your clinical judgement on what is happening
What you need from the team — urgency and action
Ms Lee is admitted with a urinary tract infection. During routine monitoring, the nurse notices:
Reduced urine output — 15 mL over last hour
Recognises sepsis with possible septic shock based on clinical indicators
Activates the emergency pathway — notifies the rapid response team immediately
Obtains observations and specimens — blood cultures, lactate, urine specimen as directed
Supports immediate treatment — IV access, fluids, oxygen commenced
Monitors response closely — documents vital signs, urine output and mental status every 15 minutes
Acting on suspicion of sepsis — before confirmed diagnosis — is best practice.

cards.title: NCLEX Readiness
cards.body: How This Maps to Your Exam

bullets.label: Sepsis and shock are high-frequency topics in
bullets.text: Sepsis and shock are high-frequency topics in the NCLEX-RN examination for internationally qualified nurses. Expect questions on:

bullets.label: Which patient should the nurse see first? Recognise life-threatening instability.
What is the most appropriate nursing action? Focus on the emergency pathway sequence.
What can be delegated, and when must the nurse escalate to the medical team?
Which finding indicates treatment is working? Understand target vital signs and lactate clearance.
Suspected sepsis demands immediate action. Do
bullets.text: Suspected sepsis demands immediate action. Do not wait for full diagnostic confirmation before initiating emergency pathways.

bullets.label: Combine perfusion markers (capillary refill,
bullets.text: Combine perfusion markers (capillary refill, urine output, lactate) with vital signs to form a complete clinical picture.

bullets.label: Bundle adherence is evidence-based. Know your local protocol and execute each step in sequence and on time.
Escalate deteriorating trends early. Use
bullets.text: Escalate deteriorating trends early. Use structured communication tools and document all actions with accurate timestamps.

bullets.label: This section has equipped you with the
bullets.text: This section has equipped you with the foundational knowledge and clinical reasoning skills to manage sepsis, shock, and multisystem deterioration confidently.

bullets.label: Recognise and respond to sepsis at the earliest opportunity
Differentiate shock types and understand their clinical implications
Support emergency bundles and time-critical interventions
Monitor, document and communicate organ dysfunction effectively
Revisit the clinical case of Ms Lee and practise applying your knowledge to similar NCLEX-style scenarios.
